item.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
item.description: The DOJ's embrace of fair use for AI training breaks with the White House's own framework, as OpenAI, Microsoft and news groups battle over copyright.
item.content:encoded:
One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

item.title: Vanity Fair writer ignites firestorm fretting 'accountability journalism' failed to take down Jensen Huang
item.description: Vanity Fair's Julia Black faces backlash after saying "accountability journalism" struggles in a culture that "does not care about accountability."
item.content:encoded:
A writer for Vanity Fair is getting intense blowback for lamenting that "accountability journalism" failed to take down scandal-plagued Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang following his shocking reinstatement on Monday. 

Nvidia made international headlines when it announced Huang would be returning as CEO just days after his resignation following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, and questions whether his company's chips were being sent to China.

The announcement came one day after The New York Times published a bombshell report alleging that U.S. intelligence had been monitoring communications between Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy the Nvidia CEO had the alleged affair with, and a Chinese spy agency.

RUBIO DUCKS QUESTIONS ON NVIDIA CEO'S REINSTATEMENT AFTER REPORTEDLY SOUNDING ALARM OVER SUSPECTED CHINESE SPY

As Jensen's return to Nvidia stunned the nation, Vanity Fair tech correspondent Julia Black appeared sympathetic to the Times reporters.

"My heart goes out to the intrepid team at the @nytimes who did absolutely generational reporting on the Nvidia scandal," Black wrote on X. "I know the feeling of trying to do accountability journalism in a culture that simply does not care about accountability. Incredibly disheartening."

She continued, "There’s a risk calculation you run every time you get a momentous tip about a powerful person. Getting the story out will mean exhausting piles of work, and sometimes considerable personal risk. You have to ask yourself whether it will be worth it—what change you actually hope to see come out of the disclosure. I’d be lying if I said the calculus on this equation hasn’t changed in recent years."

"I am of course not saying that any of these journalists wished to see a specific outcome. (I can’t speak for any of them at all!) But if it were me I would want to feel that my work was being considered thoughtfully, which this (rapid!) outcome suggests it is not. Also yes I’m aware my language is a little melodramatic but some of us still care about things," Black added.

Critics took aim at the sentiment voiced by the Vanity Fair correspondent.

"This is a very disappointing opinion expressed by someone in our industry," NBC News correspondent Tom Winter reacted. "Our job is not to condemn or to affect change. Our job is to provide the most accurate and contextually accurate information so that our audience can have informed points of view and make decisions."

"When we look to 'get' someone it leads to trouble. Should change occur as a result of the information we’ve unearthed then society / the electorate was informed and made decisions accordingly," Winter added.

"Wut? Today’s development does not discount the generational reporting that the NYT team did," CBS News correspondent Weijia Jiang wrote. "This thread implies that the journalists’ end goal was to oust Jensen Huang, which is not the case. They absolutely succeeded at holding someone in power accountable, which IS the job. How the Nvidia board responds is a totally separate issue that doesn’t change the great work they did."

Katie Miller, conservative commentator and wife of White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, reacted to Black, saying, "Reporters should never advocate for an outcome and if they do they should be fired. This Vanity Fair reporter clearly wanted Jensen out. Trust in Legacy Media will remain broken when reporters push intentional outcomes."

CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS

"What an absolutely bizarre confession for a self-proclaimed 'journalist' to express about what they see as the function and purpose of journalism," journalist Glenn Greenwald wrote.

"Please won't someone think of the journalists," RealClearInvestigations senior writer Mark Hemingway snarked.

Black offered a clarification, replying to Jiang, "I guess what I meant is that the WAY Jensen was reinstated (Trump heard lots of tech complaints/looked at stock market and didn't like what he saw) makes one question whether reporting/facts matter anymore. I'm not sure how this rushed reinstatement mid-investigation counts as accountability."

Representatives for Vanity Fair's parent company, Condé Nast, nor The New York Times, responded to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

item.title: Boston marks Thanksgiving as ‘Day of Mourning’ while historic Plymouth battles anti-Thanksgiving activists
item.description: The Boston City Council's Day of Mourning resolution honors Indigenous peoples as Plymouth officials and activists clash in court over their own observances on Thanksgiving.
item.content:encoded:
The Boston City Council recognized Thanksgiving as a "National Day of Mourning" ahead of the holiday, continuing a recurring acknowledgment from city leaders as nearby Plymouth, home of the "first Thanksgiving," battles activists in court over their Indigenous peoples observances.

Last week, the Boston City Council passed a resolution designating Thursday, Nov. 26, as a "National Day of Mourning" in Boston after it was introduced by Councilor Benjamin Weber and co-sponsored by 11 other councilors. While the resolution carries no legal weight or changes to city operations, it reflects an annual tradition for the Boston City Council, which has passed similar ceremonial recognitions ahead of Thanksgiving in previous years.

"The story of Thanksgiving that so many of us grew up learning in school fails to acknowledge the devastating consequences that colonialization had and continues to have on Indigenous peoples, " Boston City Councilor At-Large Julia Mejia said in favor of the resolution during a city council meeting on Nov. 18.

HOW VIRGINIA SCHOOL DISTRICT SHAMES KIDS TO MARK THANKSGIVING

"I think it's important that we recognize that these are not simply injustices of the past," Mejia continued. "And as a city, we have a responsibility to ensure that our commitment to equity and justice includes the Indigenous peoples whose lands we live on."

Meanwhile, in nearby Plymouth — the famed site of the 1621 "first Thanksgiving" feast between the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag people, where the United American Indians of New England (UAINE) has held the annual National Day of Mourning every year since 1970 — town officials and organizers appeared in court Monday over a dispute about this year's event logistics.

ARIZONA MAN THREATENED WITH ARREST FOR PREACHING AT HOLIDAY FESTIVAL FILES LAWSUIT

The legal battle centers on a 1998 settlement, signed after a clash between police and demonstrators the year prior, that requires Plymouth to make a mobile stage available for the event.

According to CBS Boston, town officials now say they will not set up a stage on state property without proof of insurance or an outside vendor, citing liability concerns, while UAINE argues the demand violates the decades-old agreement.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

The Plymouth Independent reported that Plymouth Superior Court Judge Brian Glenny took the arguments under advisement Monday, leaving a ruling pending just days before Thursday's 57th annual gathering on Cole's Hill. According to the outlet, Glenny did not express when a ruling might come, though lawyers involved indicated he understands "time is of the essence."

However, regardless, a UAINE leader told the Plymouth Independent that the event would continue as planned. "I can assure you we will be there Thursday," Mahtowin Munro told the local outlet.

item.title: Florida woman rocking 'Retired Drug Dealer' T-shirt got arrested on, you guessed it, several drug charges
item.description: Angela Moore, wearing a "Retired Drug Dealer" T-shirt, was allegedly found with crack cocaine, a scale, baggies and a ledger after a Florida traffic stop.
item.content:encoded:
The promise of a quieter life in retirement isn't for everyone. Some people call it a career and are able to take life in a completely different direction.

They start checking off the list of things they didn’t get to do while they were working and they don't look back. For others, it isn't that easy.

For whatever reason, they find themselves drawn back to their work. Is it a love for what they do? Is it passion and obsession that drives them?

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

That's a mystery that's hard to crack. A Florida woman rocking a "Retired Drug Dealer" T-shirt, if what the Citrus County deputies allege is true, appears to be one of those people who can't let their work go.

Angela Moore was arrested on Friday, Nov. 20, following a traffic stop for a vehicle that the Citrus County Sheriff's Office says was unable to maintain its lane, FOX 13 reports.

Moore was a passenger in the backseat of the vehicle and, as it was being searched, deputies found a cut straw on her seat. When a deputy went to retrieve it, she allegedly positioned herself between the open door and the seat.

She then asked while attempting to block his view if she could grab a jacket from inside the vehicle. That's when, thanks to her shirt, they noticed they were dealing with a retired drug dealer.

They searched a backpack belonging to Moore and allegedly found crack cocaine. But that's not all. She also allegedly had items that an active, not retired, drug dealer might have.

FLORIDA WOMAN TELLS POLICE SHE KNOWS NOTHING ABOUT DRUGS THAT ALLEGEDLY FELL OUT OF HER ‘JAIL PURSE’

Deputies said they found "a digital scale, approximately 150 unused plastic baggies and a handwritten ledger containing names and dollar amounts that investigators said were consistent with narcotics transactions."

There were more allegations made once they arrived at the Citrus County Detention Facility. The sheriff's office says that the staff at the facility found cut straws "hidden in her undergarments" that tested positive for fentanyl.

Moore, who had active warrants and was on probation during the traffic stop, now faces several drug-related charges, including possession of cocaine with intent to sell.

So much for having your feet kicked back on the beach enjoying your retirement. I'm not here to judge. Some people can't handle retirement. I get it.

item.title: TNA's KC Navarro finally gets to meet Amazing Red one-on-one with X Division Championship on the line
item.description: TNA star KC Navarro won Ultimate X at Destination X and now faces his mentor Amazing Red for the X Division Championship on Dec. 18 in El Paso.
item.content:encoded:
Total Nonstop Action Wrestling (TNA) star KC Navarro has emerged as one of the brightest wrestlers on the roster since he returned from a devastating knee injury.

Navarro put himself in a great position to capture his first championship in the company when he won the Ultimate X match earlier this month at the Destination X pay-per-view. The victory guaranteed him an opportunity against Hall of Famer Amazing Red for the X Division Championship.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Man, how many times have I fought for this title this year, right? Third time is a charm, hopefully. I've actually been talking about it. My favorite number is 21, but it seems like the number three has been my lucky number. It was my third Ultimate X," he told OutKick Dropkick. "I won this. When I wrestle Red, it'll be my third time fighting for the X Division Championship. So hopefully, third time is a charm, but I'm feeling good, man."

Amazing Red captured the X Division Championship at Bound for Glory in a seven-way scramble – the same night he was inducted into the Hall of Fame. Navarro missed his opportunity there and earlier this year at Slammiversary in an Ultimate X match.

Now, he gets a match against his mentor one-on-one. It could be a bittersweet moment for Navarro should he take the title off Amazing Red.

"It's special for sure. Red mentored me since I was 18 years old, and it's funny, when I signed with TNA in 2024, Red hit me up. He's like, ‘Yo, KC, we're gonna do our one-on-one, man,’ ‘cause we only had multi-mans, and he said, ‘We're gonna do our one-on-one, man, I'm gonna try to get booked,’ like on an indie show or like House of Glory where he usually goes, and I remember telling him no, and he was very like shocked by that ‘cause for years I was bothering him for it. But I just told him I'm like, man, like I just signed with TNA, you're one of the standards of TNA. I don't feel like I can wrestle you one-on-one unless it's for the X Division Championship or I'm X Division champion. And he respected that a lot ‘cause usually when he says he wants to wrestle somebody, they jump on the opportunity.

"I was probably one of the first people to say no, I'm not wrestling Red, and I think he was very shocked by that, especially because of our relationship. But man, to think two years later, Red’s in the Hall of Fame. Red is back. Red's X Division champion. I become No. 1 contender, and now I can say it here, December 18th, Night 1 in El Paso, it will be me versus Red for the X Division Championship. So it's very exciting. We're both very excited. It's gonna be bittersweet and I feel really good about this one."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Navarro has learned a lot from Red and he’s used his mentorship to help further his own career.

Specifically, on the height disparity between himself and some of the wrestlers he faces. TNA does feature some massive men like A.J. Francis and Special Agent Zero. But the speed of Navarro is what jumps out of the ring.

"Using my speed and that my size does not matter, ‘cause there's not a lot of guys that are me and Red's size, like we're pretty small guys, like even Nic Nemeth, who is considered small when he was over in WWE is bigger than us," he told OutKick Dropkick. "We look small compared to him. That was probably the biggest takeaways I always got from Red and to always stay humble and be grateful because this whole business could be taken away.

"There was moments where Red didn't think he was gonna wrestle again, and he stayed humble, he kept pushing, he did what he could, and now he's back. I don't think he thought that he'd be back in TNA. Here he is, and not only is he back, he's X Division champion again. So that those are probably the big things I took away from him."

Navarro’s best shot to win TNA gold will come in El Paso, Texas. The TV taping is set for Friday, Dec. 18. It will be a part of back-to-back tapings for TNA. The second will be held on the next day. Both nights will take place at the El Paso County Coliseum.

item.title: McDonald's taps into Grand Theft Auto hype with Discord ordering feature as experts share concerns
item.description: As Grand Theft Auto VI launches, McDonald's adds an "Order McDonald's" Discord feature for McDelivery via Uber Eats, but experts warn of distracted eating.
item.content:encoded:
Right on the bumper of the Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) video game release, McDonald's has launched a food ordering feature within Discord, an app widely used among gamers to talk with each other while playing.

Now, those who are still in the midst of a GTA 6 marathon can stay fueled up without too much disruption by utilizing an "Order McDonald's" option in Discord that allows players to get McDelivery through Uber Eats, entertainment outlet IGN reported.

The integration, which also includes a game called Fast-Lane Feast, is available in the Apps section of all Discord servers, channels and direct messages.

'GRAND THEFT AUTO VI' MANIA COMES WITH SERIOUS HEALTH RISKS, DOCTORS WARN

While players won't need to get up from their couch, they will probably have to pause their game, as the food ordering is done through an external Uber Eats link, IGN noted.

Fox News Digital reached out to McDonald's for comment.

The add-on has a few red flags in the eyes of some healthcare experts.

FORMER MCDONALD'S EXEC SPILLS THE BEANS ON WHY HEALTHIER MENU FAVORITE GOT THE AXE

"Making food ordering part of a gaming platform adds convenience, but it also raises questions about how food marketing and distracted eating intersect," Geremy Kerr, an Ohio-based registered dietitian, told Fox News Digital.

"Eating while absorbed in a game can make it easier to lose track of how much you've eaten."

A McDonald's Big Mac meal with a medium fry and medium Coca-Cola contains 1,170 calories, according to the company's website.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"For gamers, a practical approach is to take a break for meals, decide what and how much to order before returning to the game and keep water within reach," Kerr said.

The new feature arrives at a time when a growing number of young Americans are getting diabetes diagnoses.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

By 2060, an estimated 220,000 kids and teens are predicted to be diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recently reported.

It's possible to delay or prevent type 2 diabetes by making healthy lifestyle choices, according to the CDC.

"Gaming often means hours of sitting, and when comfort food is only a click away without ever pausing the game, the line between leisure and an unhealthy habit gets even thinner," Dr. Swapnil Patel, a physician at Hackensack Meridian Health Center in Farmingdale, New Jersey, told Fox News Digital.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"In excess, that combination can contribute to obesity, high cholesterol and type 2 diabetes."

However, that doesn't mean that someone needs to stop gaming altogether, Patel added.

"I play video games myself and enjoy comfort food at times, but I still make a point of carving out time in my schedule for exercise and my health, because enjoyment and wellness don't have to be at odds," Patel said.

Currently, the Discord add-on is only available in the U.S. in areas where McDelivery is available, cybersecurity and information outlet Cybernews reported.

item.title: Unvaccinated Pennsylvania resident dies of measles in state's ninth fatal case this year
item.description: Pennsylvania officials say an unvaccinated Centre County resident died of measles, the ninth death this year, as the state leads the nation in cases.
item.content:encoded:
Pennsylvania health officials announced Monday that a resident unvaccinated against measles died from the virus after testing positive, making it the ninth measles-related death in the state this year.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed the death less than a week after the United States lost its measles elimination status, ending a public health achievement that had been maintained since 2000.

Officials said the victim was a resident of Centre County, located in the middle of the state and most known for being home to Penn State University.

The state has 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties this year, including 49 new infections that were reported Monday.

CHILD’S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE’S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK

Hospitalizations rose from 315 to 330, according to the state’s measles dashboard. Just five of the confirmed infections involved vaccinated residents.

Last week, officials confirmed the state’s eighth measles death, an unvaccinated Clinton County resident.

Pennsylvania and federal health authorities continue to urge residents to get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, saying it the best defense against the disease.

Pennsylvania has been battling a measles outbreak since April and now leads the nation in cases, accounting for more than a quarter of all U.S. infections.

TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK BACKS MMR VACCINE, REJECTS LINK BETWEEN CHILDHOOD VACCINES AND AUTISM

The sharp rise in cases — largely in rural and Amish communities with historically low vaccination rates — has prompted state health officials to ramp up immunization efforts.

The state health department has administered more than 7,400 doses of the MMR vaccine at nearly 300 pop-up clinics. Officials plan to set up dozens more of these temporary immunization sites over the coming weeks and months.

For months, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have sparred over the response to the ongoing measles outbreak in the state.

Shapiro has accused Kennedy of spreading misinformation about the MMR vaccine and vaccines in general, something the nation's top health official has denied.

AMISH FACE NEW YORK VACCINE MANDATE IN SUPREME COURT FIGHT, MIGHT HAVE TO ‘PACK THEIR WAGONS’

Overall, Kennedy has given a mix of answers about his stance on the MMR vaccine. When testifying before the House in May 2025, he said he would "probably" vaccinate his children against measles.

When he was asked the same question in August 2024, prior to becoming HHS secretary, Kennedy said he would not give his kids the MMR vaccine.

Kennedy, meanwhile, has accused Shapiro of politicizing the outbreak and suggested that some of Pennsylvania’s reported measles deaths may have been "fabricated."

The Pan American Health Organization’s decision last Wednesday to revoke the U.S.’ measles elimination status means the virus is once again considered endemic in the country. This means it is circulating regularly at a relatively predictable level, much like the seasonal flu and chickenpox.

The difference is, measles is around 12 times more contagious than the flu and twice as contagious as chickenpox, according to Unicef.

People infected with measles — especially babies and young children — also face the risk of severe complications, including a weakened immune system or encephalitis, a type of brain swelling that can cause seizures and intellectual disabilities.

item.title: A $17 million bill for an AD who never actually started? Michigan's Trev Alberts mess gets uglier
item.description: Trev Alberts' Nebraska deposition over a civil rights lawsuit stunned Michigan Board of Regents members, leaving his $17 million MOU buyout in dispute.
item.content:encoded:
The Michigan athletic department has another problem on its hands, and it could be a very expensive one, thanks to the vetting process of what was supposed to be its new leader in Trev Alberts.

Last week, the former Texas A&M athletic director announced he was leaving the school to accept the same position at Michigan starting in December.

The move was a somewhat stunning one, as incoming Michigan Pres. C. Cybele Raver was tasked with leading this search with the help of the Board of Regents in Ann Arbor.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

So, when Alberts agreed to be the next athletic director after signing an MOU with the school over the past week, folks at Michigan were under the impression this was all but finalized.

This is where things took a turn for all parties involved, thanks to a story published last week.

The Wolverines might end up learning the hard way about what transpires when you do not complete a full background check on an incoming employee that will be tasked with also restoring an athletic department that has been marred in scandal over the past six years.

When Trev Alberts decided to accept the Michigan job, he informed Texas A&M that he was moving on to his third school in nearly six years.

Turns out, the school he had already interviewed with and accepted a job at had themselves a very big problem coming their way that pertained to Alberts' time as athletic director at Nebraska.

A lawsuit filed by a Nebraska women's basketball player in 2024 alleged that Alberts violated her civil rights by encouraging her to leave the team after not ordering an investigation into a romantic relationship the athlete had with an assistant coach.

When deposed under oath related to the lawsuit, Trev Alberts was asked if he had understood the Nebraska policy on consensual relationships under the school's personnel handbook.

According to a story by FOIABall.com, Alberts was grilled over whether he understood that coaches should not be involved in romantic relationships with student athletes.

FORMER MICHIGAN COACH SHERRONE MOORE RECEIVES PUNISHMENT FROM STALKING CASE STEMMING FROM FIRING

Did the Nebraska athletic director concede that it was ok for this situation to occur?

As outlined in his answer to the question, according to FOIABALL.com, Alberts provided this answer to plaintiff counsel.

"I mean, you know, it just depends," he added, claiming that COVID eligibility rules led to older players, who may be closer in age to coaches, which makes the situation more "nuanced."

Trev Alberts also reportedly admitted that he did not know the answer to that same question as the current leader of Texas A&M athletics.

Was this taken out of context and did Michigan react without fully understanding the way in which this was answered? That's up to them to discuss over the next few days.

But, Trev Alberts made it clear in a statement that he felt like he had been fully vetted by Michigan, after already starting to work on behalf of the Wolverines.

"The egregious characterization of words taken out of context from a deposition regarding an incident that occurred years ago is wrong and unfair," Trev Alberts said in statement. "I was informed that Michigan's General Counsel had spoken with the General Counsel of both Texas A&M and the University of Nebraska, as well as Nebraska's outside counsel, to inquire about the deposition.

"I was further told that all three of those lawyers told Michigan's GC that I had done nothing wrong or inappropriate and had followed all applicable university polices and procedures. I am proud of my long tract record of standing up for student-athletes and for following the rules and my core values."

When this story was released late last week, multiple sources tell OutKick that Board of Regents members at Michigan were shocked to learn of the answers that Alberts provided in the deposition.

On Tuesday, the University of Michigan released the following statement.

"The University of Michigan's search for its next athletic director is ongoing. As we navigate a rapidly changing landscape in intercollegiate athletics, the values that define Michigan will guide our decisions and reinforce our commitment to excellence and integrity, both in the classroom and in competition."

Given that the Wolverines were still dealing with the aftermath of the Sherrone Moore situation, which led to him being fired for having an affair with a female staffer in the football building, it was a pretty bad look for the incoming AD not to understand school policy over student-coach relationships.

Fast forward to Sunday.

The Michigan Board of Regents held an emergency call to discuss the hiring of Trev Alberts, knowing the ramifications that would be coming if made official.

This then led to incoming president C. Cybele Raver informing the board that she did not feel comfortable with the school moving forward with the hiring of Trev Alberts and needed to move in a different direction, quick.

If there is anything we've learned over the past six years regarding the University of Michigan, it's that anything is possible when it comes to a disaster of epic proportions.

Trev Alberts had already resigned from Texas A&M, which also led to him signing an MOU with the school. His contract, when fully executed, would pay him $17 million with a buyout if not fired for cause.

Was there language in the MOU that said his full hiring was contingent upon a background search? Attorneys for Alberts believe there was not that type of language, while Michigan officials are holding firm that there is an "out" for the school to avoid paying him $17 million that would come if he had been actually fired upon taking the job.

According to the contract obtained by OutKick, there is language in the MOU that says it is a "binding contract."

"Pending the completion of the Agreement this MOU shall form a binding contract between you and the University," the MOU states in the second paragraph.

Another snag for Alberts — and there are seemingly plenty — is the roughly $4 million buyout he owes Texas A&M, which Michigan agreed to cover in the MOU.

So, you have a guy that owes the Aggies millions, while at the same time fighting Michigan over what his attorneys feels as though he is owed for an MOU that might be binding.

There are plenty of things we could say about the University of Michigan and its knack for creating public relations' nightmares inside their own house, but this latest fumble by the school shows us why it's hard to give them the benefit of the doubt on anything related to athletics.

The school puts out one dumpster fire, only to start another one a few yards away.

There will obviously be a fight over buyout money related to the MOU signed by both Michigan and Trev Alberts.

All the while, Texas A&M has appointed an interim athletic director and has already started a national search for its new leader.

Just another week in college athletics.

item.title: Billy Bob Thornton urges viewers to learn the real history behind Thanksgiving on Fox Nation's 'The Mayflower'
item.description: Stars gathered in New York City for the debut screening of Fox Nation's "Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower," just in time for Thanksgiving.
item.content:encoded:
The stars were out on Monday night in New York City to celebrate Fox Nation’s "Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower" as the iconic actor seeks to educate viewers, just in time for Thanksgiving.

"The Mayflower," which is now streaming on Fox Nation, is a three-part historical docudrama that aims to strip away the myth of Plymouth Rock and inform viewers on everything from the deadly voyage across the Atlantic to Thanksgiving and one of America’s bloodiest wars. Fox News Media executives, Fox News Channel anchors, the show’s creators and other special guests gathered at The Whitby Hotel for an exclusive screening of the debut episode.

"Thank God for Fox Nation, because they’re willing to tell stories of our history, which is awesome," Thornton told the crowd.

BILLY BOB THORNTON SAYS HE’S A HOLIDAY ‘PURIST’ AS HE BRINGS BACK ‘TRADITIONAL’ THANKSGIVING AT HOME

"The Mayflower" traces the Pilgrims’ death-defying Atlantic crossing, the fragile alliance forged between the English settlers and the Wampanoag people, and the devastating conflict that ultimately transformed Britain’s colonies into the earliest foundations of an American identity.

"One of the things that I think we're quickly losing around here is our history. History is very important, and if you don't know where you came from, it's hard to live now," Thornton said.

"I love history, I’ve always studied it. My dad was a history teacher, and I always want to learn more about stuff and I didn’t know this," he continued. "I knew the story they told us in elementary school."

BILLY BOB THORNTON PUSHES BACK ON CELEBRITY ACTIVISM: ‘I DON'T KNOW ANYTHING ABOUT POLITICS’

The Academy Award-winning writer, actor and director said most people simply think, "’Oh, that’s great, the native tribe came over, and they had turkey'" — but the truth is far more complex.

"The people who came over here on [the Mayflower]… a lot of people got sick, a lot of people died," Thornton said.

He called for viewers to keep the trials and tribulations of the Pilgrims in mind when celebrating Thanksgiving with loved ones this week.

"When you say your blessings to the people, maybe remember the people that suffered to get us where we are," he said.

Fox News Media CEO Suzanne Scott, Fox News Media President and Executive Editor Jay Wallace, Fox News Media Chief Digital and Marketing Officer Jason Klarman, Fox News' Bill Hemmer, Dana Perino, Lawrence Jones, Martha MacCallum, Emily Compagno, Eric Shawn, Lisa Boothe, Paul Mauro and "House of Cards" actor Michael Kelly were among the guests for Monday’s screening and cocktail reception.

FOX NATION TEAMS UP WITH JACK CARR TO TAKE VIEWERS INSIDE THE GLOBAL MANHUNT FOR CARLOS THE JACKAL

While developing "The Mayflower," the team consulted a range of historical resources and experts, including historians at Plimoth Patuxet Museums, where portions of the series were filmed, as well as acclaimed historian Nathaniel Philbrick.

The series is produced by AIRtime Projects and Terminal B TV with Thornton as an executive producer, alongside Geyer Kosinski, Tom Forman, David Metzler, Jordan Rosenblum and showrunner and executive producer John Ealer.

"My only wish and prayer from you all is that you watch this as people who want to learn something and watch something wonderful that these wonderful producers and director put together with Fox Nation," Thornton said.

Thornton currently stars in the hit Paramount+ series, "Landman," for which he received Critics' Choice Award and Golden Globe Award nominations for Best Actor in a Television Drama. His recent projects have also included the Amazon series "Goliath" and the critically acclaimed FX series "Fargo."

item.title: Biden's first-year fundraising fails to crack 1% of Obama's library haul as questions swirl over legacy
item.description: Joe Biden raised just $1.5 million for his presidential library in 2025, per tax filings, a fraction of the $232.6 million Barack Obama brought in 2017.
item.content:encoded:
Former President Joe Biden has raised a shockingly small amount of funds for his presidential library compared to former President Barack Obama.

The figures are fueling skepticism about how history will remember Biden's single term in the White House.

In 2017, Obama’s first year out of office, the two-term president managed to bring in $232.6 million in donations and contributions to fund the foundation behind his presidential library. By comparison, Biden secured just $1.5 million in 2025 for his presidential library foundation, per tax filings.

This is less than 1% of what his former boss raised in the same amount of time after leaving office.

Even before leaving office, President Donald Trump’s library foundation has already dwarfed that of his predecessor by raising tens of millions of dollars from a variety of sources, including companies that settled lawsuits with him.

OBAMA CENTER ISN'T A TRADITIONAL PRESIDENTIAL LIBRARY. CRITICS SAY IT'S AN ACTIVISM CENTER.

Though the Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation has yet to decide on a construction site, it’s already running a deficit, spending $600,000 more than it raised in 2025. A Biden library official claimed that it wasn’t actively fundraising in 2025 in a statement shared with CBS News.

The lack of enthusiasm for Biden’s legacy has led some to claim that Americans may simply forget about his presidency as the years go on.

"Presidencies usually fade," Axios’ Zachary Basu wrote of his legacy. "But in just one year, Biden’s has been reduced to a footnote by a successor committed to dismantling every pillar of Washington’s old liberal order."

Heritage Action press manager Doug Blair told Fox News Digital, "Joe Biden spent half a century in Washington and did nothing to benefit the American people." 

"The anemic fundraising for his presidential library is a fitting bookend for a failed presidency Americans are eager to forget," he added. "Joe Biden left Americans worse off by every conceivable measure and his legacy will be a southern border blown wide open, the disgraceful image of him checking his watch as fallen American troops returned home from Afghanistan, and endless scandals and investigations surrounding him and his corrupt family.'

BIDEN'S BATTLE WITH ADVANCING CANCER RENEWS FOCUS ON PROSTATE DISEASE

Allies of the former president point to the fact that Biden presided over the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, influential pieces of domestic legislation and America’s withdrawal from Afghanistan, parts of his legacy that could contribute to historical staying power.

A January 2025 Gallup poll found that 54% of U.S. adults believed history would remember Biden as a "below-average" or "poor" president.

A source close to Biden’s foundation told CBS News that it ramped up its fundraising in 2026, pulling in multiple multi-million-dollar contributions, including two $5 million donations.

Another source told the outlet that some of Biden's close allies are frustrated that Democratic donors aren’t stepping up to support the former president’s library.

Further complicating Biden’s fundraising efforts, and his ability to nurture his public image, is his advanced age and Stage 4 prostate cancer, which has metastasized to his bones.

OBAMA CENTER OPENS AFTER YEARS-LONG SAGA AS LOCALS WARN ‘MONSTROSITY’ COULD PRICE THEM OUT

While the increase in funds is no doubt encouraging for Biden’s allies, it still puts them far behind Obama, who raised $164.8 million for his foundation in 2018.

Obama ultimately spent nearly $1 billion on his presidential library in Chicago, a sum Biden likely will not be able to reach given his current fundraising levels.

The Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation and the Obama Foundation did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

item.title: 'Worst nightmare' as Delta flight comes to sudden halt due to cabin disruption
item.description: A Delta Air Lines pilot had to stop on the taxiway at Boston's Logan International Airport right before takeoff after a passenger's cat slipped out of its carrier in the cabin.
item.content:encoded:
Passengers aboard a morning flight out of Boston faced an unusual pause on the tarmac recently after a four-legged traveler broke free in the cabin.

A Delta Air Lines flight was taxiing toward the runway at Logan International Airport on Nov. 20 when a passenger's pet slipped out of its carrier, Delta Air Lines confirmed to Fox News Digital.

The plane was preparing to depart for Tampa, Florida, when the pilot asked air traffic control for a quick stop, according to audio on ATC.com.

TRAVELERS CLASH OVER WHETHER CRUISE LINES SHOULD ALLOW DOGS AND CATS ON BOARD OR NOT

"We got a situation in the cabin. We need to hold somewhere for a minute," the captain told controllers.

"Thanks for accommodating," the captain said, according to ATC.com. "We had a cat loose in the cabin."

"That's a new one," the controller replied. "And have a good day. Meow."

The jet soon resumed taxiing, took off without further trouble and landed in Tampa on schedule, the airline said.

Steven Arroyo, a Florida-based aviation expert and a retired United Airlines captain, told Fox News Digital that pilots are required to halt takeoff procedures whenever passengers are out of their seat or if an animal gets loose in the cabin.

"It is incumbent upon the pilots to communicate what's going on in the cabin, whether it's for an animal [or] a passenger," Arroyo said. "We can't have people up and about."

He recalled a similar scare of his own in the early 1990s, when one of his dogs chewed through a nylon carrier while his family was flying from South Florida to New York.

Under the Delta Air Lines pet travel rules, small cats and dogs flying in the cabin must stay inside a closed, ventilated kennel tucked under the seat in front of their owners throughout the trip.

The airline's website warns that travelers who fail to follow pet policies or keep their animals secured inside a carrier risk losing the ability to bring pets on future flights.

The escape led to plenty of jokes and travel stories on Reddit, where users weighed in on how easily cats can slip out of carriers.

"That's the best part of the story," one commenter wrote about the air traffic controller's "meow" sound over the radio.

Several pet owners shared their own stories of animals breaking free during trips.

"My cat was always fine in her carrier. It's a backpack that has some mesh windows. Then one day she decided to unzip it and let herself out," one commenter wrote.

"I work for a wildlife agency and was called to a plane to pick up a turtle that had been found wandering the aisle by a [flight attendant] during a flight," another user shared.

Not everyone found the idea of a loose cabin pet amusing — with some travelers pointing out problems with allergies and phobias.

item.title: DOJ recovers $8B, charges more than 800 suspects in largest anti-scam surge in history
item.description: U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche says the Justice Department charged more than 800 defendants and recovered $8 billion in intended victim losses.
item.content:encoded:
Federal prosecutors have charged more than 800 defendants and recovered over $8 billion in intended victim losses as part of the largest anti-scam enforcement surge in Justice Department history, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Tuesday.

Speaking alongside FBI Director Kash Patel at a news conference in Washington, Blanche said the enforcement blitz follows President Donald Trump's March executive order directing a government-wide crackdown on fraud and predatory schemes targeting Americans. Since that directive, the Justice Department has filed more than 400 criminal cases across 85 federal districts, resulting in charges, extraditions, guilty pleas and prison sentences.

"We are not just going after individual scammers," Blanche said. "We are dismantling the criminal networks that have been stealing from the American people for far too long."

INSIDE OPERATION BLACKOUT: PATEL REVEALS GLOBAL SCAM ‘CITIES’ TARGETING YOUR PARENTS’ LIFE SAVINGS

Patel detailed the FBI's global offensive under Operation Blackout, an interagency campaign targeting international fraud syndicates. According to Patel, federal agents and international partners have seized nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, confiscated more than 14,000 digital devices and dismantled 29 scam compounds across four continents.

Those compounds operate as self-contained towns where criminal networks force human trafficking victims to run online fraud schemes against Americans, Patel said, noting that joint operations have freed more than 2,200 trafficked workers.

"They thought they could get away with it in Southeast Asia. They moved to Africa. They moved to the Middle East," Patel said. "We annihilated them on every single continent that they chose to operate and attack American citizens."

FBI OPERATION TARGETS SCAM COMPOUNDS IN AFRICA WITH ARRESTS, ACCOUNT TAKEDOWNS

The crackdown comes as online and phone fraud continue to hit U.S. households at staggering rates. Blanche cited a recent Gallup study finding that 10% of Americans reported that they or a household member fell victim to a scam in 2025, resulting in an estimated $68 billion in losses in a single year.

Officials pointed to a wide range of schemes disrupted since March, from felony inmates using contraband cellphones and handwritten scripts to run jury-duty extortion scams to Mexico-based timeshare fraud allegedly operated by major drug trafficking cartels.

In the past two weeks alone, federal authorities worked with Mexican officials to extradite a list broker accused of selling the names of more than 1 million elderly Americans to international scam networks, resulting in at least $15 million in victim losses. Agents also dismantled websites impersonating U.S. federal courts and arrested nine suspects in an alleged sweepstakes scheme that defrauded seniors of millions of dollars, Blanche said.

Overseas, a recent enforcement push coordinated in London yielded 28 arrests across Africa, $11 million in seized assets, the rescue of 120 trafficked workers and the removal of 3.7 million fraudulent Facebook and Instagram accounts, Patel said.

Beyond arrests and asset seizures, federal officials are also intervening before money leaves victims' bank accounts. Through Operation Level Up, a joint effort with the U.S. Secret Service, agents have prevented nearly $700 million in potential losses across 11,000 targeted Americans, 77% of whom did not realize they were being scammed, Patel said.

"The United States government and President Trump does not tolerate organized theft perpetrated against the American people," Blanche said. "No matter where these criminals are in the world, we will find them and hold them accountable."

item.title: Apple tightens Mac security as AI agents seek your files
item.description: Apple's macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds new Mac security controls for AI agents, letting you pick specific protected folders instead of granting Full Disk Access.
item.content:encoded:
Ever download an app on your Mac and click through the permission requests without giving them much thought? You're certainly not alone. But what if one of those approvals gave an AI assistant access to your private messages, financial documents or even files you thought were protected?

That's the concern behind Apple's latest Mac security controls. As AI agents become more capable of performing tasks on your computer, they're also requesting access to more personal information. And once you grant certain permissions, an app could potentially see far more than you intended.

Now, Apple is introducing new protections in macOS 27.3 that give you greater control over what these apps can access. The changes arrived in macOS 27.3 beta 2 on Nov. 16, with the broader software release still to come. Here's what Apple is changing and why you may want to check your Mac's privacy settings now.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS

AI assistants have become increasingly useful, especially when you want help getting through a long list of tasks. An AI agent can go further by interacting with apps and taking actions on your behalf. For example, you might ask an AI agent to organize your Downloads folder or find a receipt buried in your email. To complete those tasks, the software may request permission to access information stored on your Mac. That's where things can get uncomfortable. Some apps request a powerful macOS permission called Full Disk Access, which can give them access to nearly everything stored on your computer, including information from other apps.

Apple warns that an app with this permission can read or modify sensitive files. It may also be able to delete or export information without asking you again. And the potential exposure goes beyond documents. Another powerful permission, called System & App Protection Override, can allow an app to control your Mac and monitor activity, including keystrokes, when you grant unrestricted access. That's a lot of trust to place in software, especially when an AI agent can take actions without asking you to approve every step.

Apple's upcoming update introduces several changes designed to make powerful permissions easier to understand. It also gives Mac owners more opportunities to limit access before an app starts working.

Apple is separating its existing Device Control and Data Access permission system into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. The change helps clarify when an app is requesting permission to bypass built-in protections. Apple is also introducing more detailed warnings about the information an app could access if you approve its request. Instead of clicking through a vague permission prompt, you'll have more information about what you're allowing.

One of the biggest changes involves Full Disk Access. Starting with macOS 27.3, some apps requesting this permission will let you choose specific protected folders instead of granting access to everything. Other apps may continue using the existing approval process, depending on their purpose.

For example, an AI tool helping you organize work documents may only need access to one folder. You could grant that limited permission while keeping other protected information off-limits. Apple is also introducing a more consistent process for granting these permissions. You'll select the requesting app from a list rather than navigating different approval methods.

Another important addition gives you more control over how AI agents interact with other apps. When configuring System & App Protection Override, you can choose which apps an AI tool may control. For each approved app, you can select Ask First or At Any Time. Choosing Ask First means the AI agent must request permission before controlling that app. That extra confirmation may slow down some automated tasks, but it also gives you an opportunity to catch unwanted actions.

Apple is adding a transparency indicator that appears when an app controls another app through this permission system. That could make it easier to recognize when software is acting on your behalf.

MAC MALWARE CAN HIDE COMMANDS IN YOUR ICLOUD CALENDAR

Apple's announcement follows growing scrutiny over how much information AI-powered software can access. In September, a journalist claimed that Meta's Muse AI app had read his private messages without his permission. Meta disputed that account, saying the Messages integration requires explicit permission. Separately, a security vulnerability in OpenAI's ChatGPT Mac app could have allowed attackers to access sensitive information. OpenAI patched the flaw before it was publicly reported.

These incidents highlight the security concerns surrounding increasingly capable AI software. Even legitimate applications can create privacy risks when they receive broad access to personal information. Apple's response focuses on making those permissions more visible and giving people greater control over what they approve. Importantly, the changes won't prevent you from installing AI agents or using apps that genuinely need broader permissions.

There's something worth knowing before assuming the update will automatically protect everything on your Mac. Apple says permissions you've already granted will remain in effect after the update. The new approval experience primarily applies when apps request permissions going forward.

That means an AI app you installed months ago could still have access to information you previously approved. You'll need to review those permissions yourself if you want to change them. Apple is also allowing developers of certain backup and accessibility applications to request special permissions that preserve their existing functionality. This should help prevent legitimate tools from losing features they need to operate.

You can review your Mac's privacy permissions now, even before macOS 27.3 becomes widely available.

Steps may vary slightly depending on your version of macOS.

If you find an app with permissions it no longer needs, you can revoke its access. Depending on your macOS version, you may see a toggle or an option to remove the app from the permission list. For macOS 27.3: Select an app and click the Remove (−) button to revoke access. To replace broad access with a more limited permission, remove the app and add it again. When prompted, choose the specific protected folders or apps it needs.

Keep in mind that some legitimate applications, including backup software and security tools, require extensive access to function properly. Removing their permissions could prevent certain features from working.

AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU

You don't have to stop using AI assistants to protect your information. A few precautions can help you take advantage of these tools while reducing unnecessary exposure.

When an app requests access to your files, consider whether it needs permission to browse your entire Mac. If the new macOS controls offer a Choose Folder or Choose Apps option, use it to limit the information the software can reach. You can adjust those permissions later if the app needs additional access.

If you're using macOS 27.3, look for the Ask First setting when granting an AI agent permission to control another application. This gives you another opportunity to review what the software wants to do. It's especially useful when an AI tool interacts with apps containing sensitive personal information.

Be careful when installing new AI agents, particularly from unfamiliar websites. We've previously reported how AI-related scams target Mac owners through convincing fake download pages. Stick with official developer websites or the Mac App Store whenever possible. Keep your installed apps updated to receive security fixes.

Your Mac includes built-in malware protection, but reputable antivirus software can add another layer of security. It can help detect malicious downloads and other threats, including malware disguised as legitimate AI tools. However, antivirus software can't reliably prevent an app from accessing information you've already given it permission to use. That's why reviewing your Mac's privacy settings remains important. Even when an app has limited access to your files, you should understand how it handles information you choose to share. Check whether the developer stores your data or sends it to cloud servers. Apple's permission controls can restrict access to protected information on your Mac, but they don't replace an app's privacy policy.

An AI tool may have needed access to a particular folder when you first installed it. That doesn't mean it needs the same permission indefinitely. Periodically check Privacy & Security and remove access that no longer serves a purpose. This is particularly important for AI apps you rarely use.

If you're allowing an AI agent to organize or modify files, make sure you have a recent backup. An automated task could accidentally delete something important or change a document you wanted to keep. Apple's built-in Time Machine can automatically back up your Mac and help you recover files if something goes wrong. For step-by-step instructions, check out our guide on how to back up your computer.

I'm glad Apple is taking a closer look at how much access AI agents can have on our computers. These tools are becoming more capable, and I can see why people would want an assistant that handles repetitive work. But giving an app permission to see everything on your Mac seems like a steep price to pay for convenience. I particularly like the option to make an AI agent ask before controlling another app. That's a level of oversight I would want, especially when personal information is involved. My biggest concern is that previously granted permissions will remain active. Apple can introduce better warnings, but those warnings won't change the decisions you've already made. I'd encourage Mac owners to spend a few minutes reviewing their settings rather than waiting for the next update.

item.title: Draft plan to overhaul Smithsonian spotted on White House staffer's laptop: report
item.description: A commuter's photos of a White House adviser's laptop show a draft plan to overhaul the National Museum of American History, ProPublica reported.
item.content:encoded:
Photos taken by a commuter on Washington, D.C.'s Metro system appear to show a White House advisor’s laptop displaying a draft plan to overhaul the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, ProPublica reported.

Last month, a commuter riding the Orange Line from Northern Virginia noticed a man in a suit working on a laptop displaying a document titled "Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan." The commuter photographed the screen and sent the images to ProPublica.

The multipoint draft proposed firing museum Director Anthea Hartig, creating new museum-wide exhibit guidelines that omit the Smithsonian’s diversity style guide, reviewing its traveling-exhibition strategy — including ending "The Bias Inside Us" — and reassessing grants to what the draft called "woke third parties," including the American Alliance of Museums. A separate handwritten note that was also pictured proposed a policy against "X-rated" exhibitions. ProPublica said it likely referred to an exhibit the White House criticized for displaying a two-piece chrome-and-rubber harness designed for sadomasochism.

INSIDE THE BEHEMOTH SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM NETWORK DRAWING FIRE FROM THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION

The draft renewal plan pictured on the staffer's laptop surfaced amid a broader Trump administration effort to reshape how the Smithsonian presents American history. The White House released a 162-page report on July 4 accusing the National Museum of American History of "ideological capture." Two congressional hearings followed, and a July executive order directed officials to post signs outside the museum informing visitors of the report’s findings about "ideological capture," though ProPublica reported the signs had not yet gone up as of publication.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment on the photographed document and whether any of its proposals are under consideration, but did not receive a response by publication. The photographed document does not establish whether the proposals were approved or put into effect.

TRUMP GIVES SMITHSONIAN DAYS TO REPLACE 'STRANGE MODERNIST SCULPTURE' WITH FOUNDING FATHER

ProPublica reported that it identified the White House staffer as Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy advisor with the White House Domestic Policy Council — which produced the July report — after spotting the initials "B.S." or "S.B." on the laptop screen and following a man matching his description from the Metro to a White House employee checkpoint. ProPublica reported that Bock did not respond to its messages and that the Smithsonian declined to comment.

ProPublica reported that the proposals on Bock’s laptop envisioned a permanent exhibit celebrating Western civilization, a display on prominent American families, a large George Washington statue at the museum entrance and new museum-wide interpretive guidelines written without reference to the Smithsonian’s diversity style guide. A separate handwritten note photographed alongside the laptop also floated a potential new D-Day exhibit.

In addition to the proposed exhibit changes, the draft called for the firing of National Museum of American History Director Anthea Hartig and about a dozen senior administrators and curators. That proposal came as Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch, who leads the broader institution, was preparing to retire at year’s end. ProPublica reported that White House criticism of the Smithsonian helped prompt Bunch’s departure.

TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED

The draft plan also called for overhauling the museum’s online curriculum for K-12 students, including dropping a module on immigration and creating new material focused on the Founders, according to ProPublica, which noted the document floated possible titles for the new curriculum, including "Architects of Liberty" and "Profiles in Liberty."

The administration’s push to reshape how the Smithsonian presents American history began picking up steam in March 2025, when Trump signed an executive order directing Vice President JD Vance, through his role on the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, to help remove what the order called "improper ideology" from the institution. The Smithsonian, which encompasses 21 museums and D.C.'s National Zoo, is governed by a 17-member Board of Regents that consists of the vice president, the chief justice of the Supreme Court, members of Congress and private citizens. It receives more than $1 billion in federal funding annually.

The White House’s July report cited, among other examples, a museum exhibit that raised the possibility Benjamin Franklin had used enslaved people in his household as subjects in electrical experiments. It also criticized staff training based on a social-action toolkit that the report said linked museums to White supremacy and other forms of oppression.

The report said the museum should not erase slavery, Jim Crow or other national failures. Its broader charge was that the museum was not giving visitors a coherent account of how the country developed, including both its achievements and its wrongs.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

The criticism from the Trump administration came amid a longer-running debate over how the museum should tell the nation’s story, which has stretched back to at least 2001.

ProPublica reported that in response to earlier criticism, the Smithsonian convened a blue-ribbon commission in 2001, whose 2002 report urged the museum to present a more unified account of American history. The outlet also reported that after George Floyd’s murder in 2020, Bunch and other leaders began an institution-wide reassessment of the Smithsonian’s priorities and how it tells the nation’s story.

item.title: Body washed ashore in Oregon identified as former city councilor missing since September plane crash
item.description: Human remains that washed ashore on the Oregon coast were identified as Ralph H. Busby III, whose plane crashed into the Pacific Ocean in September.
item.content:encoded:
Human remains that washed ashore along the Oregon coast last week have been identified as a 78-year-old former city councilor whose small plane crashed into the Pacific Ocean in September.

The Oregon State Medical Examiner's Office confirmed on Monday that the remains were identified as Ralph H. Busby III, FOX12 Oregon reported. Busby served on the Newport City Council from 2013 to 2017, the city said in a statement posted to its Facebook page on Monday.

Busby was the lone occupant of a twin-engine Beechcraft B95 that crashed about a mile west of Nye Beach near Newport shortly before 12:45 p.m. on Sept. 21, according to the U.S. Coast Guard Northwest District.

4 FLORIDA FAMILY MEMBERS FOUND DEAD AFTER SMALL PLANE GOES DOWN OFF THE BAHAMAS

Eyewitness Yoshio Abe, who was fishing just south of the Yaquina Head Lighthouse, told the outlet in September that he noticed the plane flying unusually low, about 20 feet above the water, in a strange flight pattern before it hit the ocean.

"Within three minutes the head went down, and in 10 seconds the whole thing went down," Abe said.

The Coast Guard deployed a helicopter and search-and-rescue boats and covered around 124 square miles before suspending the search later that night.

The body was discovered in the surf near Yaquina Head Lighthouse on Nov. 15, Oregon State Police said. Weather and hazardous surf conditions kept state police and U.S. Coast Guard crews from recovering the remains for three days until the body washed ashore.

FLORIDA LEARJET CRASH INVESTIGATORS DIG UP ENGINE PIECE AFTER PILOTS WARNED OF ROUGH WEATHER AHEAD

Oregon State Police told the outlet that the National Transportation Safety Board has been notified as investigators continue looking into the Sept. 21 crash.

After officials identified the remains, the City of Newport posted its statement extending condolences to Busby's wife, Sharon, his family and friends. City officials noted his work on the Budget, Airport and Vision 2040 advisory committees and his advocacy for the Newport Municipal Airport.

"His dedication to the community and his willingness to give his time and experience helped guide Newport's future," the city said in its statement.

"We are grateful for Ralph's years of service to Newport and the lasting impacts he made on our community," it continued.

item.description: Benjamin Angus Carpenter faces first-degree intentional homicide in wife Erica Carpenter's death as prosecutors cite texts about "powdery" water.
item.content:encoded:
A Wisconsin man has been charged with killing his marathon-running wife more than two years after she died in an alleged basement fall – with prosecutors pointing to texts about "powdery" water, an ominous Google search and a new girlfriend.

The West Allis Police Department said Benjamin Angus Carpenter, 45, has been arrested and charged with first-degree intentional homicide in the October 2024 death of his wife, Erica A. Carpenter, 40.

Officers were dispatched to the couple's residence in the 2900 block of South 95th Street around 10:38 p.m. on Oct. 13, 2024, for a welfare check after a report that Erica had fallen and was bleeding from the head, according to a criminal complaint.

TEACHER FOUND DEAD WITH THROAT SLIT; DETECTIVES SCRUTINIZE HUSBAND’S SHIFTING STORY

When officers arrived, they found Carpenter performing CPR on his wife at the bottom of the basement stairs. Officers took over lifesaving efforts until rescue personnel arrived and transported her to Froedtert Hospital, where she was pronounced dead at 5:14 the next morning.

Carpenter told investigators Erica had felt dizzy and was having trouble breathing all day before collapsing while they were doing laundry in the basement, claiming they tumbled backwards down the stairs while he tried carrying her up and that she struck her head against a cinder block wall.

Police launched a death investigation that spanned more than two years, reviewing autopsy findings alongside searches of email accounts and cellphones before concluding Carpenter planned and caused her death.

While Erica's final cause of death was ruled undetermined, Milwaukee County Deputy Chief Medical Examiner Douglas Kelley told detectives her injuries – including neck cartilage fractures and hemorrhage – were suspicious for asphyxia and indicated blunt force trauma to the neck, the complaint states.

Investigators also questioned Carpenter about his background as a Brazilian jiu-jitsu black belt and whether choke submissions leave marks, to which he replied, "not that I've ever heard of."

Toxicology testing detected doxylamine, an over-the-counter sleep aid, and hydrocodone, a prescription opioid painkiller, in Erica's system. Less than two weeks before her death, Carpenter had texted Erica asking her to research melatonin or other sleep remedies for them – messages that were later deleted from his phone, investigators found.

‘AMERICAN IDOL’ CONTESTANT’S 100K TEXTS WITH MISTRESS SHOW MOTIVE IN WIFE’S MURDER, PROSECUTORS SAY

On the day Erica died, Carpenter searched Google for "can I crush pills and take them in water," prosecutors alleged.

Weeks earlier, on Sept. 18, 2024, Erica had confronted Carpenter over text about something in her drink, writing, "And what the f--- have you been doing to my water the past few days?!?!?" before adding, "There's been powdery s--- in it at least twice now."

Instead, his actions immediately after Erica's death painted a far different picture. The couple's son told investigators he was introduced to his father's new girlfriend the very next day when she brought dinner over. Financial records pointed to a similar contradiction in the weeks right after Erica's funeral. Carpenter made his initial court appearance Nov. 18, where a court commissioner set his cash bond at $500,000 and placed him under JusticePoint Level 5 supervision with no firearms or dangerous weapons if released, court records show.

item.description: Elizabeth Smart reveals Brian David Mitchell planned to kidnap seven young girls under a "seven diamonds plus one" ideology she says was pure control.
item.content:encoded:
Elizabeth Smart, who survived a harrowing nine-month kidnapping as a teenager, opened up about her captor Brian David Mitchell's disturbing plans to abduct seven young girls as part of a twisted religious system.

"He had a whole plan to go out and kidnap seven young girls," Smart told Sean Hannity on his "Hang Out With Sean Hannity" podcast.

Smart explained that Mitchell and his wife followed an ideology centered on what they called the "seven diamonds plus one," which included their own set of scriptures and assigned roles to the women and girls involved.

POLYGAMOUS SECT LEADER CONVICTED ON STATE CHARGES AFTER GIRLS FOUND IN UNVENTILATED TRAILER

"She [the wife] was the one. And her role, her calling in life was to be the mother of Zion," Smart recalled. "She was the true queen. And I was her handmaiden. And I was just the first of the seven."

Smart became one of America's most recognized child abduction survivors in 2002 after being forced from her Salt Lake City bedroom at knifepoint at age 14. Mitchell, a self-proclaimed prophet who called himself Immanuel David Isaiah, dragged her to a remote, dilapidated campsite in the woods, where his wife and accomplice, Wanda Barzee — who went by Hephzibah — was waiting.

Barzee washed Smart’s feet, then tried to remove her pajamas. Mitchell declared, "I hereby seal you to me as my wife before God and His angels as my witnesses." When Smart screamed, Mitchell threatened to kill her.

NANCY GUTHRIE UPDATE: 25 WEEKS AFTER ABDUCTION, ELIZABETH SMART SAYS THERE'S 'REASON TO HAVE HOPE'

During her nine months in captivity, Smart endured repeated sexual assaults, was restrained and confined in a dark space and was forced to eat garbage. She was also subjected to pornography and forced to drink alcohol until she vomited, then left lying in her own vomit.

Mitchell was convicted in federal court in 2010 and sentenced to life in prison in 2011. Barzee pleaded guilty and was released from prison in 2018.

Now a child safety activist, Smart regularly speaks on behalf of missing and exploited children, drawing on her own experiences to help survivors of abuse.

During her conversation with Hannity, Smart reflected on the ideology Mitchell used to justify his actions, suggesting his beliefs were a means of manipulating those around him rather than genuine belief.

"I think he just wanted to rape little girls, but I think this is just how he was able to control Wanda Barzee," she said.

Smart also said her religious upbringing was one of the reasons Mitchell singled her out, believing he could use her faith and young age to manipulate her.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy prosecutors ask court to delay her retrial in children's stranglings
item.description: Plymouth County prosecutors are asking the state's highest court to pause Lindsay Clancy's March retrial while her double jeopardy appeal plays out.
item.content:encoded:
With the clock ticking toward Lindsay Clancy's March retrial in the strangling deaths of her three children — and the judge's mandatory retirement in June — it's Plymouth County prosecutors who are asking Massachusetts' highest court to pause the proceedings while her defense raises a double jeopardy appeal.

"The full Court will presumably determine whether such a retrial will violate the defendant’s double jeopardy rights," wrote Assistant Plymouth County District Attorney Melissa Johnsen. "As such, it makes little sense to move forward with proceedings intended to bring the defendant to a trial, where this Court may ultimately decide that a retrial is barred by double jeopardy."

Johnsen added that it would be "ambitious" to believe the appeal would be resolved in time for jury selection in her retrial, currently scheduled for March 29.

LINDSAY CLANCY TO BE RETRIED FOR MURDER IN KILLING OF THREE CHILDREN

Clancy's lawyers, Kevin Reddington and Martin Weinberg, have opposed the idea, writing to the state's Supreme Judicial Court that "she wants to keep her trial date."

While prosecutors had argued that a stay in the trial court would "forego any additional expense and effort" in preparations, Clancy's lawyers countered that "the cost of a stay would fall on Ms. Clancy, who is held without bail."

LINDSAY CLANCY'S LAWYER REVEALS POST-MISTRIAL STRATEGY AS RETRIAL LOOMS

Her appeal centers on the argument that it wasn't necessary for Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial with jurors deadlocked 11-1 on Sept. 4, and as a result she is facing unconstitutional double jeopardy with the case slated for a second trial.

PROSECUTORS REVEAL SIX LINDSAY CLANCY JURY NOTES AS THEY FIGHT BID TO DISMISS MURDER CHARGES

The lone holdout, whom other panelists accused of ignoring reasonable doubt and insisting Clancy was guilty anyway, could have been replaced with an alternate, according to Reddington.

Michael Desronvil, the only juror who voted to find her guilty, has denied such allegations and said in a recent Fox News interview that he believed Clancy had meticulously planned to murder her children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — while her then-husband was running errands.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Sullivan wrote that he was skeptical of the other jurors' allegations, denied the defense request to replace Desronvil and declared a mistrial after a week of stalled deliberations. Then he denied defense motions to hold an inquiry into Desronvil, finding that it would be inappropriate to interfere with jury deliberations, and another motion to dismiss the case on double jeopardy grounds.

LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL HOLDOUT SAYS HE THOUGHT SHE WAS 'METHODICAL' IN THE 'EXECUTION' OF HER CHILDREN

The defense appealed to Justice Elizabeth Dewar, who last week referred the case to the full Supreme Judicial Court. Plymouth County prosecutors asked the court Monday to stay the retrial as her appeal plays out.

"The prosecution's position is probably based on the difficulty of deciding a full bench appeal and getting ready for trial No. 2 so quickly," said Jack Lu, a retired Massachusetts judge and legal scholar who has been following the case. "I see this as a reasonable request, and the parties have not even publicly stated, after setting the actual trial date, that they will really be ready."

Prosecutors will likely have to recruit a new team of experts and revise their approach after the first trial ended with 11 of the 12 jurors siding with the defense.

Under Massachusetts law, Sullivan will reach the age of mandatory retirement in June, prompting some experts to question whether prosecutors are aiming to delay the retrial long enough to try it under a new judge.

"The biggest question is are your experts locked in," Lu said. "So, I do not think they are judge shopping which, contrary to what some believe, is a part of litigation."
